requirement: Short links expire after a week. Redirect analytics are retained indefinitely. Expired links should still redirect for trusted partners.

clarificationDecisions.affectedPath: Requirement 1.1 ('The system SHALL cause a short link to expire exactly 7 days (168 hours) after its creation timestamp') states a precise timing bound but never defines what the observable, testable consequence of expiration is for a standard (non-trusted) requester — e.g., whether the redirect endpoint returns an HTTP 404, a 410 Gone, a redirect to an error/landing page, or whether the underlying record is deleted versus merely flagged inactive.
clarificationDecisions.question: At exactly the 168-hour boundary instant, is the link still-valid (inclusive) or already-expired (exclusive)?
clarificationDecisions.answer: At exactly the boundary the link is expired (validity is exclusive of the instant), consistent with the existing ExpiryPolicy rule.

clarificationDecisions.affectedPath: Requirement 1.3 ('...when the requester is identified as a trusted partner...') uses 'trusted partner' without defining which requesters qualify — no criteria (contractual designation, named allowlist, account tier, etc.) are given for who counts as a trusted partner.
clarificationDecisions.question: How is a request identified as coming from a trusted partner, and which actor maintains that determination?
clarificationDecisions.answer: API-key / signed-header based, consistent with the existing creator-auth model; maintained by the system's existing auth/partner administration.

clarificationDecisions.affectedPath: Requirement 1.3 grants a security-relevant expiration bypass to 'trusted partner' requesters but names no actor responsible for designating, granting, or revoking trusted-partner status, nor any actor who maintains that classification over time.
clarificationDecisions.question: How is a request identified as coming from a trusted partner, and which actor maintains that determination?
clarificationDecisions.answer: API-key / signed-header based, consistent with the existing creator-auth model; maintained by the system's existing auth/partner administration.

clarificationDecisions.affectedPath: Requirement 1.3's phrase 'identified as a trusted partner' implies a request-time identification/authentication step but specifies no mechanism (e.g., API key, mutual TLS, IP allowlist, signed header) by which the system is supposed to perform that identification.
clarificationDecisions.question: How is a request identified as coming from a trusted partner, and which actor maintains that determination?
clarificationDecisions.answer: API-key / signed-header based, consistent with the existing creator-auth model; maintained by the system's existing auth/partner administration.

clarificationDecisions.affectedPath: Requirement 1.3's clause 'continue to redirect an expired short link' for trusted partners states no duration or ceiling on how long past the 168-hour mark the bypass remains in effect — it could mean indefinitely, or up to some further limit.
clarificationDecisions.question: At exactly the 168-hour boundary instant, is the link still-valid (inclusive) or already-expired (exclusive)?
clarificationDecisions.answer: At exactly the boundary the link is expired (validity is exclusive of the instant), consistent with the existing ExpiryPolicy rule.

clarificationDecisions.affectedPath: Requirement 1.1 asserts an unconditional, exact expiration ('SHALL cause a short link to expire exactly 7 days (168 hours) after its creation timestamp') with no stated exception, while Requirement 1.3 establishes that expired links continue to redirect for trusted-partner requesters — meaning the system does not, in fact, uniformly enforce the 'exactly 168 hours' bound R1.1 states as an absolute rule.
clarificationDecisions.question: At exactly the 168-hour boundary instant, is the link still-valid (inclusive) or already-expired (exclusive)?
clarificationDecisions.answer: At exactly the boundary the link is expired (validity is exclusive of the instant), consistent with the existing ExpiryPolicy rule.

downstreamImpactAnalysis.reason: S5-S12 were all BLOCKED (never executed) at the moment the clarification was recorded -- proven per-node below -- so the real, honest downstream-impact analysis is that nothing needed replanning. ReplanService's own downstream-invalidation walk (T096) was deliberately NOT invoked: it does not distinguish already-executed work from never-started work, so calling it here would have invalidated work that was never attempted, and no proven mechanism exists to re-dispatch fresh work afterward (appendReplannedEdges is only ever exercised, in ReplanServiceTest, to prove cycle rejection -- never a real resumption). Resumption instead used the same governed approve-and-continue path T132/DS-A already uses.

s6RealResponse.design: No requirement text, titles, or descriptions were supplied for requirements 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 — only opaque task IDs (T1-T6), their dependency edges, and requirement-ID tags. Absent that content, this design documents the three-workstream shape implied by the dependency graph itself, without inventing domain specifics: (1) Requirement 1.1 is realized by T1→T2, a define-then-build pair — T1 establishes the requirement's foundational artifact (e.g. a schema, interface, or module skeleton) and T2 depends on it to implement the requirement's behavior on top of that foundation. (2) Requirement 1.2 is realized independently by T3→T4, the same define-then-build shape, with no dependency on the 1.1 workstream — these two tracks can proceed in parallel. (3) Requirement 1.3 is realized by T5 (which, like T1 and T3, has no upstream dependency and stands as 1.3's own foundational unit) converging with T6, which depends on both T2 and T5 — meaning T6 is an integration task that composes the completed 1.1 behavior with the 1.3 foundation to deliver requirement 1.3's full behavior. Recommended module boundaries: three independently deployable/testable units for 1.1, 1.2, and 1.3, with an explicit integration seam at T6 where the 1.1 and 1.3 units compose. T3/T4 (requirement 1.2) has no consumer among the other five tasks and no consumers depend on it, so it should be built and verified as a fully self-contained slice. Before implementation starts, the actual requirement text for 1.1/1.2/1.3 and a description of what T1-T6 each build must be obtained — this design cannot specify concrete components, data models, or algorithms without it, and proceeding to build against guessed content would risk building the wrong thing.
s6RealResponse.contractImpact: No API surface, schema, or contract can be identified or assessed because no requirement content, endpoint names, or data shapes were provided. If requirement 1.3's integration task (T6) exposes a boundary between the 1.1 output (from T2) and the 1.3 foundation (from T5), that boundary is the one contract point implied by the graph and should be defined explicitly (its shape, versioning, and error semantics) as part of T5 or T6 before either is implemented, since T6 cannot be built against an undefined interface. No impact to pre-existing contracts is asserted here, since no existing contract was referenced.
